A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reward-feature model research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, references, and appendices are readable, and retained experiments can be matched despite extensive revision and relocation.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A report original reward-model training, preference-prediction, adaptation, and best-of-n experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix B report original experiments with synthetic users, reward-model raters, UltraFeedback, and PersonalLLM, including additional sensitivity and robustness results.

M1.justification: The shared reward features, user-specific linear weights, joint training, and frozen-feature adaptation remain. However, v2 Equation (6) prints logarithms of raw score differences without the sigmoid present in v1 Equations (6)–(8), while still describing logistic regression. The PDFs do not resolve whether this is solely a formulation error or a changed intended objective.

E1.justification: V1's three scenarios using four-dimensional Gaussian preference profiles are largely replaced by a population defined through 13 structural, syntactic, and semantic features with binary likes/dislikes. V2 also adds PersonalLLM evaluation with ten reward-model raters. The UltraFeedback reward-model experiment and UF-P-4 comparison remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds Park et al.'s nonlinear comparators with three- and five-layer MLPs, removes v1's full-model adaptive baseline, and adds the linear baseline to the UltraFeedback reward-model comparison (v1 Figure 5 versus v2 Figure 4a). Gemini, GPT-4o, and VPL comparisons remain.

E3.justification: The main evaluation changes from three fixed held-out users to 500 sampled users, with revised adaptation budgets and test aggregation. V2 extends validation-based checkpoint selection beyond v1's reward-model experiment and scales training with rater count. Its in-context evaluation changes the prompt and averages original and reversed response orders (Appendices B.1–B.2).

E4.justification: Beyond v1's feature-dimension and adaptation-size comparisons, v2 adds systematic rater-count and preference-homogeneity sweeps, distribution mismatch with held-out homogeneity fixed at 0.65, and adaptation using one, three, or five examples. It also tests nonlinear baselines with 100 examples and investigates in-context failures using helpfulness-based preferences (Figures 5–8 and Tables 1–3).

E5.justification: Confidence levels change from 95% to 99%, including the retained UF-P-4 and reward-model plots. New main experiments report five independent training/adaptation runs, whereas v1 generally used two training runs with five adaptations each. The retained reward-model experiment still reports ten combinations, and UF-P-4 retains five adaptation seeds; this does not establish that all retained experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: V1's three-scenario results are replaced by population-level results, alongside new PersonalLLM and robustness findings. V2 Table 2 reports accuracy 0.7053 for RFM(32), 0.6258 for the baseline, and 0.6285 for the linear baseline with ten adaptation examples. These changed settings do not establish performance gains over v1. The VPL comparison retains 61.61% for RFM versus 61.49% for VPL.

T1.justification: V1 contains Bradley–Terry derivations and a preference-selection argument. V2 adds grouped non-i.i.d. sampling, bounded-loss assumptions, PAC bounds, covering-number and Rademacher analyses, and proofs of four propositions in Appendix A. However, Proposition 2's setup and proof use different worst-case variance definitions: single-example loss variance versus variance of per-rater averages.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now foreground formal analysis, PAC bounds, and guidance for allocating preference-collection resources. V2 claims a first rigorous treatment under its assumptions and emphasizes dependence on rater count and preference heterogeneity. V1 primarily presents RFM and its practical personalization advantages.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of within-user versus between-user variation, data-allocation tradeoffs, and an explicit limitation concerning training complexity versus adaptation simplicity. It proposes explanations for in-context failures and conjectures greater benefits with actual individuals than with aggregated reward-model proxies. The broader-impact discussion is substantially retained in Appendix D.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds feature construction, normalization, sampling, adaptation, nonlinear-baseline, and PersonalLLM pairing details. V2 reports releasing the UltraFeedback reward-model labels and explains why training scripts are unavailable. Documentation remains inconsistent: Appendix B.1 lists rater counts 20/40/60/80/100, whereas Figure 6 lists 4/16/36/64/100. V1's explicit filtered UltraFeedback sample counts are also omitted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning around concurrent PReF and LoRe work, acknowledging the same or closely related architecture and distinguishing its learning analysis from their optimization and empirical contributions. Section 6 and Appendix C add extensive discussion of these works, Park et al., Zhong et al., and policy-composition approaches.

P1.justification: The abstract, background, personalization analysis, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten around the theoretical framework. The former three-scenario organization and standalone Discussion disappear; related-work detail moves into an expanded Appendix C, broader impact moves to Appendix D, and a conference checklist is added.

P2.justification: The paper changes from two-column to single-column formatting and substantially rebuilds its main experimental displays. V2 adds three tables and multiple analysis plots, and summarizes reward-model comparisons in new bar charts. Retained curves are relocated: v1 Figure 5 becomes v2 Figure 11, and v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figure 10.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens empirical support through 500 sampled users, PersonalLLM, controlled sensitivity and distribution-shift tests, and reported label release. However, the rewritten loss omits the sigmoid, and the new central PAC analysis uses inconsistent variance definitions between its setup and proof. Conflicting rater-count settings also impair reproducibility. These substantive empirical benefits coexist with unresolved mathematical problems affecting a principal new contribution, preventing a reliable overall net-quality judgment.
